identification.name: Maraging Steel 300 (DMLS, Aged)
identification.common_form_notes: Supplied as gas-atomised powder for direct metal laser sintering (DMLS/SLM), printed into near-net-shape parts then post-machined as needed. Not available as conventional wrought stock in this condition — see a wrought/conventionally-processed maraging 300 entry for bar/sheet stock properties.
identification.notes: Mechanical properties are from an EOS manufacturer datasheet for MaragingSteel MS1 printed on an EOS M 300-4 DMLS (Direct Metal Laser Sintering) system, in the aged/heat-treated condition — the intended final-use state (print, then age-harden; comparable to the H1025-vs-Condition-A distinction already noted on the 17-4 PH entry in this database). The exact aging recipe, per EOS's official MaragingSteel MS1 Material Data Sheet: solution anneal 2 h at 940°C (±10°C), rapid air cool to below 32°C, then age 6 h at 490°C (±10°C) for peak hardness — lower aging temperatures (up to ~630°C) trade strength for toughness, per that document's hardness-vs-aging-temperature curve (54 HRC (Rockwell C hardness) at 490°C down to ~44 HRC at 630°C). Hardness (54 HRC) is stored using this peak-aging value, since it matches the same recipe used for the strength data. As-printed (pre-aging) properties from the EOS M300-4 datasheet are notably weaker and more ductile: tensile 1100–1200 MPa, yield 860–980 MPa, elongation 12–13% (vs. ~2100 MPa, ~2000 MPa, ~3.5% aged) — a dramatic strength/ductility tradeoff from the aging step, and worth knowing if a part must be used as-printed. The source reports mechanical properties separately for vertical and horizontal build orientation (an AM (additive manufacturing)-specific anisotropy consideration): aged tensile 2110 MPa (vertical) / 2120 MPa (horizontal), aged yield 1990/2040 MPa, aged elongation 3.0%/4.0% — the stored values are simple averages of the two orientations rather than either one specifically, since the difference is small in the aged condition (larger before aging). EOS's official multi-system datasheet independently reports very similar aged properties for a related system (EOS M 290, 40 µm layers): yield 2010–2020 MPa, tensile 2085–2100 MPa, elongation 4–4.5% — good cross-validation of the M300-4-specific numbers stored here, and also reports a heat-treated fatigue strength of 650 MPa (ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 12107 statistical estimate, not tied to a specific cycle count, so not stored as an S-N curve point). Reported process quality: 0.050% porosity, ~90 µm typical pore size, 50 µm layer thickness — i.e. a well-optimized, nearly fully-dense (>99.9%) print; density is otherwise not expected to differ meaningfully from wrought stock. Young's modulus (190 GPa) is independently confirmed by both a separate MatWeb datasheet for conventionally-processed (annealed) 18Ni-300 and EOS's own official datasheet (heat-treated) — exact agreement. CTE (coefficient of thermal expansion) uses EOS's official multi-point table (ASTM (American Society for Testing and Materials) E228, heat-treated), preferred over the single-value MatWeb figure for the annealed wrought condition. Poisson's ratio, density, and thermal conductivity remain from the annealed wrought MatWeb source, since EOS's official datasheet doesn't report them and they aren't expected to vary meaningfully between wrought and AM processing of the same base alloy (unlike strength/hardness, which are highly aging-condition-dependent). Shear strength derived via von Mises: UTS (ultimate tensile strength)/√3 = 2115/1.732 ≈ 1221 MPa. Ferromagnetic, like other iron-nickel martensitic steels. Weldable — a genuine advantage of maraging steels over conventional Q&T (quenched-and-tempered) ultra-high-strength steels, since the low-carbon martensite doesn't form the brittle high-carbon martensite that causes weld cracking in those alloys. Weld in the solution-annealed (pre-aging) state, then age the whole part (including the weld/HAZ (heat-affected zone)) afterward — welding an already-aged part will locally over-age/soften the HAZ. Even with proper post-weld aging, a peer-reviewed study (Materials 2024, 17(2), 440) found the HAZ retains measurably lower ductility and toughness than the base metal — embrittlement from coarsened prior-austenite grain size and intergranular cracking along packet boundaries — so welded joints in fatigue-critical or high-reliability applications should be qualified/tested rather than assumed equivalent to the base metal.

typical_usage: High-strength, low-porosity DMLS/SLM-printed parts needing near-tool-steel strength with better toughness than conventional through-hardened tool steel: tooling inserts, high-strength brackets/fittings, and functional prototypes where geometry (internal channels, lattices, topology-optimized structures) isn't achievable with wrought stock. Requires access to a metal AM system and a post-print aging furnace cycle to reach the properties shown here — as-printed parts are much weaker until aged.
